extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) and counsel involved in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria used by the USPTO (ALJ and Director/OED) to evaluate practitioner misconduct and to determine sanctions in disciplinary proceedings under the PTO Code and PTO Rules (37 C.F.R. parts 10 and 11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. §10.23(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation by, inter alia, making changes to the [application], pre-filing and during prosecution, without his client's knowledge or authorization (charged under 37 C.F.R. §10.23(b)(4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: unilaterally altering application drawings/claims (e.g., replacing parallel perforations with diverging/angled perforations) without adequately informing the client; misleading client about the content/scope of claims; ALJ found such behavior to constitute deceit/misrepresentation. The decision cites dictionary definitions (e.g., 'deceit' = 'dishonest behavior'; misrepresentation includes oral/written conduct and concealment); non-disclosure or concealment may have the effect of a misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. §10.23(b)(5); 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice, e.g., offering to pay and paying money to a client in exchange for the client refraining from filing an ethics grievance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision treats procuring a promise not to file a disciplinary grievance (or paying to secure such silence) as obstructing the disciplinary process and contrary to public interest; cites case law (In re Blackwelder; In re Wallace; In re Abrams) and states such behavior undermines self-policing and transparency. It is explicitly unethical to buy the silence of a dissatisfied client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct that adversely reflects on practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office (37 C.F.R. §10.23(b)(6); 11.804(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging in conduct that adversely reflects on a practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office, such as making unauthorized changes to an application and arranging quid pro quo refunds to avoid grievances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts that indicate unfitness (pattern of misrepresentation, concealment, or attempts to avoid discipline) weigh against practitioner and support disciplinary sanctions; this charge was applied where the practitioner both altered the application without disclosure and negotiated payments to prevent grievances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowingly giving false or misleading information to a client (37 C.F.R. §10.23(a) and (b)(c)(2)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowingly giving false or misleading information to a client in connection with any immediate, prospective, or pending business before the Office, e.g., assuring a client a patent would be obtained despite prior art obstacles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision treats affirmative assurances of patentability that disregard known prior art (or the practitioner's own prior drafting that creates a barrier) as knowingly misleading and sanctionable. Knowledge or willful blindness, especially by an experienced practitioner, aggravates culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misrepresentation through concealment or non-disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Concealment or even non-disclosure may have the effect of a misrepresentation; misrepresentation is not limited to written or spoken words but includes any conduct that amounts to a false assertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion quotes Black's Law Dictionary and prior disciplinary precedent to emphasize that failing to point out material changes (or hiding them) can be equivalent to affirmative misstatements. Practical example: not telling a client that drawings/claims were materially changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to communicate and to devote proper attention to client matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners have an obligation to communicate adequately with clients and to devote proper attention to legal matters entrusted to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document cites prior Letter of Caution admonishing the practitioner to communicate; failure to inform a client of material changes and to ensure meaningful client review is a ground for discipline. The ALJ viewed the practitioner's misleading assurances and lack of communication as violation of fiduciary duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conditioning refunds or settlements on client's agreement to forego filing grievances
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper to offer or condition refund/settlement terms on the client's agreement to withdraw or refrain from filing disciplinary complaints or ethical grievances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision treats refund arrangements made in exchange for a client's agreement to 'tear up any and all paperwork prepared to file any [ethical] complaints' as prejudicial to the administration of justice; partial refunds that fall short of full restitution and are tied to silencing the client are aggravating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof: violations proven by clear and convincing evidence (37 C.F.R. §11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of the PTO Code or PTO Rules must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director and ALJ apply the clear-and-convincing standard to findings of misconduct. The decision affirms ALJ findings where the record provides ample factual support under that standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for exclusion or suspension (37 C.F.R. §11.54(b)(1)-(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: When imposing exclusion or suspension the adjudicator must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client/public/legal system/profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused; and (4) existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ALJ must explain reasons for imposing sanction after weighing these four factors. The decision applies them: finding duty violations, intentional/knowing conduct, actual injury to client, and aggravating factors (no mitigating factors present) to support exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and mitigating factors (examples used by the USPTO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors include prior disciplinary history, indifference, delay in restitution, failure to acknowledge wrongdoing, and extensive experience used to exploit knowledge; mitigating factors (if any) should also be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision emphasizes practitioner's extensive prior disciplinary history and pattern of similar misconduct as significant aggravating factors; absence of remorse or full restitution also aggravates. These factors affect severity of sanction (here, exclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of depositions and role of parole-evidence rule in disciplinary proceedings (37 C.F.R. §§11.39(c)(4), 11.51(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Depositions may be taken in lieu of personal appearance upon a showing of good cause and admitted under conditions deemed appropriate by the hearing officer; parole-evidence rule does not bar client testimony in an attorney disciplinary matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision permits admission of a videotaped deposition for impeachment and core-issue evidence; it notes that the parole-evidence rule is inapplicable in disciplinary proceedings where testimony is used to address misconduct rather than to enforce contract terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal standards to the USPTO Director (37 C.F.R. §§11.55(f), 11.56(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: On appeal from an ALJ Initial Decision, the USPTO Director may conduct a de novo review of the factual record and may affirm, reverse, modify, or remand the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director reviews the ALJ record and may make independent findings; constitutional challenges to the disciplinary scheme may ultimately be addressed in Article III court after exhaustion of administrative remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice obligations after public discipline (37 C.F.R. §11.59)
rubrics_metrics.description: When imposing public discipline, the OED Director/USPTO must give notice of the public discipline and reasons to disciplinary enforcement agencies in the jurisdictions where practitioner is admitted, to courts where practitioner is admitted, and to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision orders such notices as part of the remedy; this is a routine consequence of public discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of disciplined practitioner (37 C.F.R. §11.58)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplined practitioners must comply with the procedural duties and restrictions set forth in 37 C.F.R. §11.58 following discipline by the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order requires compliance with §11.58 (e.g., restrictions on practice until reinstatement); noncompliance can lead to further sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible remedies and administrative actions (examples imposed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies include exclusion from practice before the USPTO (patent, trademark, non-patent matters), dissociation of practitioner's name from Customer Numbers and PKI certificates, prohibition on applying for or being added to Customer Numbers until reinstated, and public notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision explains and orders these specific administrative remedies as appropriate sanctions for the misconduct found; ALJ/Director should tailor relief consistent with the §11.54 factors and record.
